title: The Hawk and the Hen
author: Visayan folk tale
source: Public domain. Retold in English from the Visayan folk tale collected in Mabel Cook Cole's Philippine Folk Tales.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Long ago in the Visayan islands, a grand hawk flew down from the mountains to see the world. In a farmyard by the sea, he spied a beautiful young hen scratching in the sun, and he circled down to meet her.

segments.speaker: hawk
segments.text: "Good day, lovely hen! I am the hawk of the high mountains. Will you promise to marry me?"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The hen was so flattered that a fine mountain hawk would ask her that she clucked out a promise without thinking twice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The hawk was delighted. He gave her a shining ring to wear on her wing and flew home to the mountains to prepare the wedding feast.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the hen had quite forgotten one thing: she had already promised to marry the rooster of her own farmyard! When the rooster saw the ring on her wing, he ruffled up all his feathers.

segments.speaker: rooster
segments.text: "COCK-A-DOODLE-WHAT?! A ring? From a HAWK? You gave your promise to ME first, long ago!"

segments.speaker: hen
segments.text: "Oh dear, oh dear! You are right! What a forgetful hen I am!"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The hen was so ashamed that she threw the hawk's ring far into the tall grass, so she would not have to look at it. But oh — when the hawk came flying back with wedding gifts, and saw her wing bare —

segments.speaker: hawk
segments.text: "Where is my ring? You have thrown away my ring AND your promise! A promise, little hen, is not a thing to scratch into the dirt!"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The hen hung her head and searched the grass, but the ring was gone. The hawk circled overhead and called down his judgment,

segments.speaker: hawk
segments.text: "Until you find my ring, you shall scratch the ground and search — you and all your children after you. And whenever I remember my lost ring, I shall swoop down to your farmyard and take a fat young chicken as payment!"

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And so it is to this very day. That is why hens and their chicks are forever scratch-scratch-scratching at the ground — still searching for the hawk's lost ring. And that is why, when the shadow of a hawk crosses the farmyard, the mother hen cries out and gathers her chicks beneath her wings.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The wise old folks of the Visayas tell this story to remind their little ones: do not make a promise you cannot keep — and if you make one, guard it well, for a promise is the most precious ring of all.
